first-call.title: Your first model call: it's just an API
first-call.description: Learn to call a model from your backend, read the usage field, and survive a 429.
first-call.html:
You have done this before

You have called Stripe to charge a card. You have called Twilio to send a text. Both were an HTTP POST with a secret key, and both sent JSON back.

An LLM is the same thing. You POST some text, and it returns JSON with more text. No math, no GPUs, no training.

It is just slower and metered. One call can take 5 to 30 seconds, and you pay for every word in and out.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: calling the provider from the browser with the key in the bundle. Also: retrying a 429 in a tight loop, which only makes the limit worse.

Best practice: a small backend route holds the key, calls the provider, and backs off on 429. Check stop_reason too. "max_tokens" means the answer was cut off.

  • An LLM call is an HTTP POST that returns JSON, like Stripe or Twilio.
  • The API key lives in a server env var, never in the browser.
  • usage gives token counts for your bill; stop_reason: "max_tokens" means the answer was cut.
  • On 429, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, not in a tight loop.

tokens.title: Tokens and the context window
tokens.description: Learn to estimate tokens, budget the context window, and avoid the "prompt is too long" error.
tokens.html:
Why did a 40-page PDF break the chat?

A user uploads a 40-page contract and asks a question. Your backend sends it all. The provider answers 400 Bad Request: prompt is too long.

You know body-size limits. Express has limit: '1mb' and nginx has client_max_body_size. Models have one too. It is counted in tokens, not bytes.

A token is a chunk of text. It can be a word, part of a word, or one symbol. About 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 English words.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: trimming with text[:32000] or text.slice(0, 32000). Characters are not tokens. You can cut a JSON object in half, and Bangla or code can still overflow.

Best practice: count tokens with a tokenizer on the server before you send. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so use the right one, or the provider's token-count endpoint.

  • A token is a chunk of text. 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 English words; code and Bangla use more.
  • The context window is one budget: system + history + documents + max_tokens.
  • Going over returns 400. Count tokens on the server before you send.
  • You pay for every input token on every call, so trim history and send only what is needed.

sampling.title: Temperature and top-p: the randomness dials
sampling.description: Learn to pick temperature and top_p for a task, and explain why extraction needs temperature: 0.
sampling.html:
Same input, different JSON

Your invoice parser sends the same PDF twice. The first reply has "total". The second has "amount_due". Your code crashes on the second one.

Nothing is broken. The model samples each token from a list of options. Two request settings control how random that draw is: temperature and top-p.

Once you see the mechanism, choosing the values is easy.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: running extraction, routing or classification at temperature 0.7 or higher. You get different keys and labels on each run, and bugs you cannot reproduce.

Best practice: use temperature: 0 for anything your code parses. Keep 0.7–1.0 for chat replies and drafts. Temperature 0 is very stable, but not a promise. Still validate the JSON.

  • The model scores every next token (logits); softmax turns scores into probabilities.
  • temperature divides the logits: 0 is greedy and repeatable, higher is flatter and more random.
  • top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens that reaches p and cuts the odd tail.
  • Use 0 for extraction, routing and classification; 0.7–1.0 for creative text.

streaming.title: Streaming answers with SSE
streaming.description: Learn to stream model tokens from FastAPI to the browser, and keep proxies from breaking it.
streaming.html:
Your chat endpoint takes 20 seconds. Users leave after 3.

A model writes its answer one token at a time. A long answer takes 5 to 30 s. If your API waits for the whole thing, the user stares at a spinner. Then a wall of text lands at once.

Worse, proxies and load balancers often give up after 30 to 60 s. Long answers turn into 504 Gateway Timeout.

The fix is old web tech: stream the answer as it is written, over SSE.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: await the full completion, then return it. Users wait, and proxies time out.

Best practice: an async generator that yields one SSE event per delta. Add X-Accel-Buffering: no so nginx skips proxy buffering for this route.

  • Generation takes seconds. Buffered replies mean a spinner, then a wall of text, then sometimes a 504.
  • Stream token deltas as SSE events: data: {...} plus a blank line. TTFT drops under a second.
  • FastAPI: StreamingResponse around an async generator. Browser: fetch plus res.body.getReader(), or EventSource for GET.
  • If streaming "does nothing", check the proxy: turn off proxy buffering.

structured.title: Structured outputs you can trust
structured.description: Learn to get JSON from a model that never crashes your API, and validate it at the boundary.
structured.html:
"Return valid JSON" works 199 times. Then it doesn't.

You ask a model to pull vendor and total from invoices. The prompt ends with "Return valid JSON". It passes every test.

In production, one reply in a few hundred arrives wrapped in a Markdown code fence. Another has a trailing comma. Another forgets total. JSON.parse throws, and your route returns a 500.

The fix has two layers: structured output from the provider, and a schema check in your code.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: JSON.parse(completion.text) straight into your database. One odd reply becomes a 500 or, worse, bad data.

Best practice: one schema, used twice. Send it to the provider as the structured output format. Validate the reply with the same schema in your code.

  • "Return valid JSON" in a prompt is a wish. At scale you get fences, trailing commas and missing fields.
  • structured output with constrained decoding masks invalid tokens, so the shape is guaranteed.
  • Still validate at the boundary with Pydantic or Zod: types, ranges, enums.
  • Never JSON.parse raw model text without a try/catch and a schema.

embeddings.title: Embeddings: meaning as coordinates
embeddings.description: Learn to explain what an embedding is, rank documents by cosine similarity, and avoid the two classic traps.
embeddings.html:
The user typed "money back". Your doc says "Refunds".

Your help center has a page called "Refund policy". A user searches "how do I get my money back". WHERE title ILIKE '%money%' finds nothing. No words match.

An embedding fixes this. A model turns each text into a fixed-length list of floats, for example 1,536 of them. Texts with similar meaning get nearby lists, even with zero shared words.

You search by "nearby", not by "equal".

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: store only the vector. Months later you switch embedding models. Old and new vectors mix in one table, and search quietly returns junk.

Best practice: store the model name with every vector, filter on it, and re-embed everything when you switch. Here it is with pgvector in FastAPI.

  • An embedding is a fixed-length float array, e.g. 1,536 numbers. Nearby means similar meaning.
  • cosine similarity = (u·v)/(|u||v|). Near 1 means same direction, so same meaning.
  • Pure vector search blurs exact strings like SKUs and IDs. Add keyword search later (hybrid search).
  • Store the model name with each vector. Switch models? Re-embed everything.

chunking.title: Chunking: cutting documents the right way
chunking.description: Learn to split a document into chunks that keep each fact whole, and store the metadata you need for citations.
chunking.html:
The bot cannot find a fact that is right there

Your help page says "Refunds take 5–7 business days." A user asks the support bot how long refunds take. It says "I don't know."

The page was indexed. So what went wrong? The page was cut into chunks before it was turned into embeddings. The cut landed in the middle of that sentence.

Chunking is the first step of every search-over-your-docs feature. Get it wrong and nothing later can fix it.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: store only the chunk text and its vector. Later the bot answers, but cannot say where the answer came from. You also cannot filter by product or delete one page's chunks when it changes.

Best practice: split on headings, then store metadata next to every chunk. It is just more columns in the same row.

  • Fixed-size cuts slice sentences and tables, so a fact ends up in two weak chunks.
  • Overlap repeats a little text across borders. Make it at least as long as a sentence.
  • Best: split on structure (headings, code blocks), about 200–800 tokens per chunk.
  • Store metadata (source URL, title, section) in the same row for citations and filters.

pgvector.title: Storing vectors in Postgres with pgvector
pgvector.description: Learn to store embeddings in Postgres, query the nearest ones with <=>, and pick the right index for production.
pgvector.html:
You do not need a new database

You have 100,000 chunks, each with a 1,536-number embedding. You need the 5 closest to a question, in a few milliseconds.

You might think you need a special vector database. You probably already run one: Postgres. The pgvector extension adds a vector column type and a distance operator.

The search is plain SQL: ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5. The hard part is the same as always: picking the right index.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: build the index with one distance and query with another. The index below is for cosine (<=>), but the query uses <-> (L2). Postgres silently skips the index and scans every row.

Best practice: pick one distance and use it everywhere. For most text embeddings that is cosine: vector_cosine_ops in the index, <=> in the query. Build IVFFlat only after loading data; prefer HNSW.

  • pgvector turns Postgres into a vector database: a vector(1536) column and plain SQL.
  • ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5 returns the 5 nearest chunks by cosine distance.
  • With no index, every query scans every row: fine at 1,000 rows, slow at 100,000.
  • Use HNSW with vector_cosine_ops in production. IVFFlat needs data first and drifts as you insert.
  • Query with the same operator the index was built for, or the index is skipped.

rag.title: RAG: answering from your own data
rag.description: Learn to build a RAG pipeline that finds the right chunks with hybrid search and answers with citations instead of guesses.
rag.html:
The model has never read your docs

A customer asks your bot: "What is the warranty on SKU-4471?" The model was trained on the public web. It has never seen your product pages. So it guesses: "2 years." That confident guess is a hallucination.

RAG fixes this with a step you already know: a database query. Find the chunks that answer the question, paste them into the prompt, and tell the model to answer only from them.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: paste the chunks under the question and hope. When retrieval misses, the model fills the gap from memory and sounds just as sure.

Best practice: number each chunk with its source. Tell the model to answer only from them, cite them, and say "I don't know" otherwise. Now a retrieval miss is an honest "I don't know", not a hallucination.

  • RAG = search your data, put the best chunks in the prompt, answer only from them.
  • Vector search misses exact strings like SKUs and error codes. Add BM25 for hybrid search.
  • Merge the lists with RRF, then let a reranker pick the best few.
  • Prompt rules: answer only from context, cite sources, say "I don't know" otherwise.

tools.title: Tool calling: the model asks, your code acts
tools.description: Learn to register a tool, run the model's tool call safely in your backend, and send the result back.
tools.html:
Your chatbot cannot see your database.

A customer asks: "Where is order 4417?" The LLM has never seen your orders table. On its own it can only guess, or make something up.

Tool calling fixes this. You describe functions the model may ask for. The model replies with a request, not an answer. Your code runs the real query and hands back the result.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: JSON.parse the args and pass them straight to the database. A prompt like "refund order 9001 for $5,000" can steer the model into a call you never meant to allow.

Best practice: validate with a schema (Zod or Pydantic), check permissions for this user, and return an error string instead of throwing. The model can read the error and try again.

  • You register tools as name + description + JSON Schema parameters.
  • The model replies with a tool call: a name plus arguments as a JSON string. It never runs anything.
  • Your backend validates and authorizes the args, like any request body, then runs the real code.
  • The result goes back as a role: "tool" message. Errors go back as readable strings, not crashes.

agent-loop.title: The agent loop (ReAct) and its guardrails
agent-loop.description: Learn to explain the agent loop and add the guardrails that stop runaway loops and double side effects.
agent-loop.html:
One tool call is not enough.

A customer writes: "Order 4417 arrived broken. Email me a return label." The model must look up the order, then send an email, then reply. That is three model calls, and it decides the order.

An agent is just a loop around tool calling. Call the model. If it asks for tools, run them, append the results, and call it again. If it does not, you are done. This is the ReAct loop: reason, act, repeat.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake 1: returning "Error". The model cannot fix what it cannot read, so it loops.

Mistake 2: retrying a side effect. If the email went out but the reply timed out, a retry sends a second email.

Best practice: say what failed and what to do next. Give side effects an idempotency key, so a retry is idempotent. Ask the user before risky actions like refunds.

  • An agent is a loop: call the model, run the tools it asks for, append results, repeat.
  • The loop ends when a reply has no tool calls, or when it hits max_iterations.
  • Vague errors cause blind retries. Say what failed and what to do next.
  • Side effects need an idempotency key, and risky actions need a human "yes".

mcp-obs.title: MCP and tracing: plug in tools, see every step
mcp-obs.description: Learn to connect tools through MCP servers and read a trace to find the slowest and the most expensive step.
mcp-obs.html:
Three services, three piles of glue code.

Your agent works. Now the team wants it to read GitHub, query Postgres and post to Slack. By hand, that is three sets of schemas, auth and wrappers. Then the next AI app needs them all again.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard plug. An MCP server exposes tools. Any MCP client connects over stdio (a local process) or HTTP. It asks tools/list, then tools/call. It speaks JSON-RPC.

Common mistake → best practice

Mistake: flying blind. Your logs say "agent answered in 14 s" and nothing else. You cannot tell which step was slow or why the bill tripled.

Best practice: wrap every model call and tool call in a span with OpenTelemetry. Record tokens and cost as attributes. Send spans to Langfuse, Arize Phoenix or LangSmith, just like an APM. Also: only connect MCP servers you trust, with least-privilege credentials.

  • MCP servers expose tools. Any MCP client can list and call them, so you skip custom glue per service.
  • Transport is stdio for local servers and HTTP for remote ones. The messages are JSON-RPC.
  • A trace has one span per model call and tool call, with time, tokens and cost.
  • Sort spans by duration to fix slowness. Sort by tokens to fix the bill.

evals.title: Evals: unit tests for AI
evals.description: Learn to score an AI feature on a golden dataset and block a bad prompt change in CI.
evals.html:
You changed one line. Is it better?

You edit the system prompt to fix one bad answer. It looks great in your three manual tries. You ship it.

A week later, support says refund answers are making things up. Your one-line change broke 40 other questions. Nobody noticed, because nothing checked.

In normal code, tests catch this. AI features need tests too. They are called evals.

Common mistake: the "vibe check"

Mistake: you try three questions in a playground, they look fine, you ship. Then a model upgrade quietly breaks 20% of answers.

Best practice: a script that scores the golden set and exits non-zero below the bar. CI runs it on every pull request. Libraries like Ragas or DeepEval give you ready-made graders. A 30-line script works too.

  • Evals are unit tests for AI: a golden dataset, graders that score, and a CI gate.
  • Code checks verify shape: JSON, citations, length. An LLM-as-a-judge grades meaning.
  • Track faithfulness, context recall and answer relevance.
  • Run on every prompt, model or code change, and fail the build below the bar.

cost-cache.title: Cost, latency and prompt caching
cost-cache.description: Learn to estimate an AI feature's daily cost and cut it with prompt caching, prompt order and model routing.
cost-cache.html:
The demo cost $3. Production costs $324 a day.

Your demo ran 100 times. Then 10,000 requests a day arrive and the bill jumps. Before you panic, look at what you send.

Each request repeats the same 8,000 tokens: system prompt, docs, tool schemas. Only 300 tokens change. You pay full price for the same bytes, 10,000 times a day.

Cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price. Output tokens usually cost about 5× more.

Common mistake: dynamic data at the top

Mistake: a template string puts the time and user name first. Every request is unique, so the cache never hits.

Best practice: static first, dynamic last. Cap max_tokens, since output is the expensive part. Route easy tasks to a small model. Cache whole answers for repeated questions, keyed by a hash of the normalised question.

  • Cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price. Output costs more per token.
  • Prompt caching reuses an identical prefix: cheaper input and lower TTFT.
  • Static first, dynamic last. A timestamp at the top busts the cache.
  • Cap max_tokens, route easy tasks to a small model, cache repeated answers.

choose-approach.title: Prompt, RAG, fine-tune or local? Choosing well
choose-approach.description: Learn to pick prompt, RAG, fine-tuning or a local model for a real feature, and run a model locally with Ollama.
choose-approach.html:
"Should we train our own model?"

Your manager read an article and asks: "Should we fine-tune our own model?" It sounds impressive. It is usually the wrong first move.

Most features need the model to know your facts and answer in a fixed shape. A strict system prompt plus RAG and structured output does both. About 90% of real use cases stop there.

The other tools are real, but for narrow jobs. You pick them by asking three questions.

Common mistake: fine-tuning to teach facts

Mistake: fine-tuning on your docs so the model "knows" them. It still mixes facts up, and every doc edit means retraining.

Best practice: RAG for facts, a strict prompt for rules, and evals to prove it. When data must stay inside, run an open-weight model with Ollama. A 7B model at 4-bit quantization needs about 5–8 GB of memory. A 70B one needs 40 GB or more.

  • Start with a strict prompt and structured output. Add RAG for private or fresh facts.
  • Fine-tune with LoRA only for a fixed style or format at scale, never for facts.
  • Go local with Ollama or vLLM for privacy, offline use, or cost at huge volume.
  • You now have the full path: call, ground, act, test, cache, choose. The rows below are the minimal stack.

cap-scaffold.title: Step 1: Scaffold DocsBot
cap-scaffold.description: Learn to set up the DocsBot repo with a FastAPI health check, a Next.js page that shows "API: ok", and secrets that git never sees.
cap-scaffold.html:
Start with a skeleton that runs

Every later step adds AI to DocsBot: streaming, RAG, tools, evals. Each one is easier to debug when the plumbing already works.

So step 1 has no AI at all. A Next.js page calls a FastAPI GET /health and shows API: ok. Your keys live in a .env file that git ignores from day one.

Write the code: the API

Settings come from env vars and .env, never from the code. The API has one route for now.

Write the code: the page and the secrets

The page is a client component: it fetches in the browser and shows a badge. NEXT_PUBLIC_ values ship to every visitor, so put URLs there, never keys.

  • DocsBot is two apps: FastAPI in api/ on :8000 and Next.js in web/ on :3000.
  • Settings come from env vars and .env via pydantic-settings, never from code.
  • CORS must allow the exact page origin, http://localhost:3000. curl ignores CORS; browsers do not.
  • .env is git-ignored; .env.example is committed with names only.

cap-chat.title: Step 2: Stream your first answer
cap-chat.description: Learn to stream model tokens from POST /chat to the page over SSE, measure TTFT, and survive a 429 or a missing key.
cap-chat.html:
Nobody waits 8 seconds for a blank box

A full answer can take 5 to 10 seconds. If the page shows nothing until the end, users think it broke.

With SSE, the API forwards each token as the model writes it. The first word shows in under a second. That delay is TTFT, and it is the number users feel.

Write the code: the streaming API

One client, built from settings. max_retries and timeout handle a busy or stuck provider before the stream starts.

Write the code: the stream reader

The browser reads the body chunk by chunk. A chunk can end mid-event, so keep the leftover and wait for the blank line.

  • stream_chat() yields each text delta from one AsyncOpenAI client built from settings.
  • POST /chat sends data: {"type":"delta",…} lines, then data: [DONE].
  • The page reads with getReader(), splits on blank lines, and times TTFT.
  • max_retries handles 429 and 5xx; timeout stops hangs; a 401 means fix the key and restart.

cap-schema.title: Step 3: Typed answers end to end
cap-schema.description: Learn to end every stream with one typed answer event, checked by Pydantic on the server and Zod in the browser.
cap-schema.html:
Text is for people, types are for code

The page now shows streamed text. Soon it also needs data: follow-up questions now, citations in step 5.

If that data is a loose dict, one renamed field breaks the UI in silence. So every stream ends with one answer event that matches a schema. Pydantic checks it on the way out, and Zod checks it on the way in.

Write the code: the schema on the server

Stream plain text for speed, then make one small structured output call for follow-ups. The model's JSON must match the Followups schema.

Write the code: the Zod mirror

Same fields, same defaults. safeParse never throws, so bad data hides the extras instead of crashing the page.

  • Answer(text, citations, followups) is one contract, in Pydantic and in Zod.
  • The server streams deltas, then sends one validated answer event, then [DONE].
  • Follow-ups come from a small structured output call; if it fails, they are just [].
  • The browser uses safeParse: bad data hides extras, it never crashes the page.

cap-ingest.title: Step 4: Index your docs
cap-ingest.description: Learn to run Postgres with pgvector in Docker, and index your Markdown docs with one safe, re-runnable command.
cap-ingest.html:
DocsBot has never read your docs

Right now DocsBot answers from the model's memory. It has never seen your docs, so it guesses.

In this step you load them into Postgres. You split each Markdown file into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding, and store it with pgvector. When you're done, one command indexes docs/, and running it twice is safe.

Write the code: the database

Run Postgres in Docker, then create the table once with a migration. The tsv column is a generated tsvector, so keyword search needs no Python code.

Write the code: ingest.py

Split on headers, cut long sections into overlapping windows, embed in batches, and replace each file's rows in one transaction.

  • Postgres + pgvector runs in Docker. One migration adds the table, an HNSW index and a GIN index on the generated tsv.
  • Split on headers, then into ~500-token windows with 50 overlap. Keep source, title and section as metadata.
  • Embed in batches and check the size: the model's vectors must match vector(1536).
  • Delete-then-insert per file in one transaction makes ingest idempotent.

cap-rag.title: Step 5: Cited answers
cap-rag.description: Learn to answer questions from your own docs with hybrid search, numbered sources and citation chips that link to the source.
cap-rag.html:
Make the chat read before it answers

Your docs are in Postgres, but /chat ignores them. Ask about error E1043 and the model guesses.

In this step /chat searches first. hybrid search picks the best 5 chunks, the prompt numbers them, and the model must cite them. Answers get chips that link to the source. A question your docs can't answer gets an honest "I don't know".

Write the code: app/retrieve.py

One SQL query does both searches and the RRF merge. Then number the sources, and keep only citations you really sent.

  • hybrid_search runs a vector CTE and a keyword CTE in one query and merges them with RRF (k = 60).
  • Vector search catches paraphrases; keyword search catches exact codes. You need both.
  • Number the sources [1]..[5]. The rules say: answer only from them, cite, or say you don't know.
  • The server keeps only citations whose n was sent. The UI turns them into chips.

cap-agent.title: Step 6: Let DocsBot act: a guarded ticket tool
cap-agent.description: Learn to let DocsBot open a support ticket through a tool loop with a step cap, a confirm step and an idempotency key.
cap-agent.html:
From answering to doing

Sam writes: "My invoice is wrong. Can someone look?" DocsBot can quote the billing docs, but it can't help Sam yet.

In this step it learns one action: open_ticket. Three guards keep it safe: a step limit, a "yes" from the user before anything runs, and an idempotency key so a double-click never makes two tickets.

Write the code: the table and the tool

First the side effect itself. The database, not the UI, enforces "one ticket per key". The model only sees subject and email. The server makes the key.

Write the code: the loop and the confirm step

The loop asks the model, validates any tool call, and stops at MAX_STEPS. A valid call does not run. It becomes a confirm event, and only /chat/confirm runs the tool.

  • Tools are a JSON-schema list (TOOLS). The model only asks; your code validates with Pydantic and decides.
  • The loop stops at MAX_STEPS = 4. Bad args go back as readable errors, so the model fixes them or asks the user.
  • Nothing with side effects runs until the user clicks Confirm on the confirm event.
  • An idempotency key with UNIQUE and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes double-clicks and retries safe.

cap-ship.title: Step 7: Ship with confidence: traces, evals, caching
cap-ship.description: Learn to trace every request, block bad prompt changes in CI with evals, cache the prompt prefix, and run DocsBot with one docker compose up.
cap-ship.html:
Will it still work next week?

DocsBot works on your laptop today. But next week someone tweaks the prompt "to sound friendlier". Does it still stick to your docs, or is that a silent regression?

In this last step you add the safety net real teams use: a trace for every request, an eval suite that blocks bad pull requests, prompt caching to cut cost, and one docker compose up to run it all.

Write the code: traces and evals

Traces show what happened in one request. Evals show if quality held across 20. evals/run.py talks to the API over HTTP, the same contract the UI uses, and exits 1 under 0.90.

Write the code: CI, caching and ship

CI runs the same evals on every pull request. Then two small changes make DocsBot cheaper and easy to run anywhere.

  • You built a real AI product: streaming chat, typed answers, hybrid RAG with citations, a guarded tool, traces and an eval gate.
  • @observe() turns each request into a trace: one span per step, with latency, tokens and cost.
  • run.py grades 20 golden questions with code checks and a strict LLM-as-a-judge at temperature 0. CI blocks merges under 0.90 faithfulness.
  • Static prefix first, changing parts last: that order makes prompt caching work.
  • For your portfolio README: a 30-second demo GIF, the architecture board, docker compose up steps, your eval scores with the CI badge, a trace screenshot, and what you would build next.
